# The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models

###### Abstract

While Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated striking
capabilities on frontier mathematical problems, it remains unclear
whether they possess the structural mathematical understanding
underlying their solutions. In this paper, we take a first step toward
systematically studying mathematical understanding in LLMs, from
diagnosing its distinct capabilities to leveraging these findings to
improve post-training. First, we introduce the notion of Mathematical
Primitive to probe structural mathematical understanding and propose
Prim, a novel benchmark that evaluates mathematical reasoning along four
distinct dimensions: Discovery, Generation, Digestion, and Execution.
Second, our systematic diagnosis shows that solution accuracy masks
distinct capability profiles, primitives unlock substantial latent
execution capacity, and Discovery is the dominant bottleneck in
mathematical reasoning. Our post-training analysis further shows that
discovery-limited failures are particularly amenable to repair. Finally,
building on these findings, we introduce Absorb, a primitive-privileged
self-distillation framework that selectively transfers primitive-guided
reasoning into the student model. Extensive experiments demonstrate that
Absorb consistently improves mathematical reasoning over baselines
across model scales and challenging benchmarks.

## 1 Introduction

Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have driven rapid
progress in mathematical problem solving, with frontier models
increasingly capable of tackling research-level questions and, in
several recent cases, resolving or making substantive progress on
long-standing open problems ([OpenAI, 2026d](#bib.bib9); [OpenAI,
2026c](#bib.bib15); [Claude, 2026](#bib.bib14); [Bubeck et al.,
2025](#bib.bib17); [Jang and Ryu, 2025](#bib.bib16)). Yet these striking
successes leave unresolved a more foundational question: what models
actually understand about the problems they solve and the mathematical
content of the solutions they produce. Successful problem solving does
not necessarily imply such understanding: models may arrive at correct
answers through specious deductions ([Boye and Moell,
2025](#bib.bib10)), while conversely identifying sound high-level proof
structures yet failing in low-level technical execution ([Lu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib11); [Qin et al., 2025](#bib.bib12)). Existing works
provide limited insight into this disconnect, as mathematical reasoning
is still assessed primarily through outcome-level metrics such as
final-answer accuracy or formal proof verifiability, obscuring whether
success reflects the discovery of the mathematical structure needed for
a solution or merely the successful execution of a derivation.

Understanding mathematical reasoning therefore requires more than
verifying that a derivation is correct; it requires exposing the ideas
that organize the argument—why it works, which components are essential,
and what can be generalized or reused. This need becomes increasingly
salient as LLM-generated proofs grow in scale and complexity: lengthy
chains of valid steps may establish correctness while leaving the
underlying mathematical structure difficult to identify. Recent work has
begun to emphasize precisely these aspects of mathematical reasoning,
calling for representations that reveal the motivation, structure, and
key ideas underlying an argument rather than only its final
outcome ([Frieder et al., 2024](#bib.bib13)). In his ICM 2026 lecture,
Terence Tao similarly highlighted the importance of making
machine-generated mathematics conceptually digestible ([Tao,
2026](#bib.bib18)), warning that optimizing primarily for formal
correctness risks producing an increasing volume of valid but opaque
proofs without a corresponding increase in mathematical understanding.
For LLMs, this perspective shifts the focus from merely producing valid
proofs to determining whether the structural knowledge organizing those
proofs is actually accessible to the model.

In this paper, we systematically study structural mathematical
understanding in LLMs, as illustrated in
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models"):
the ability to identify the compact, load-bearing mathematical structure
that explains why a solution works, distinct from the procedural ability
to generate the derivation itself. We operationalize this notion through
the Mathematical Primitive, a concise, non-procedural representation of
the foundational idea organizing a solution, and introduce Prim, a
benchmark spanning four complementary dimensions: Discovery, Generation,
Digestion, and Execution. Our diagnosis reveals that ❶ similar solving
accuracy can mask markedly different capability profiles, ❷ correct
primitives unlock substantial latent execution capacity, and, most
importantly, ❸ independent Discovery is the dominant bottleneck to
mathematical reasoning. We further find that discovery-limited failures
are substantially more amenable to post-training, but existing methods
can introduce regressions on problems the model already solves.
Motivated by these findings, we introduce Absorb, a post-training
paradigm that uses Mathematical Primitives as privileged information and
a bounded override mechanism to selectively transfer their guidance into
the student’s reasoning process, enabling primitive-guided reasoning to
be internalized without access to primitives at inference time. Our main
contributions are as follows:

- •
  Benchmarking structural mathematical understanding. We introduce the
  notion of Mathematical Primitive and propose Prim, a benchmark that
  evaluates mathematical reasoning across four complementary dimensions:
  Discovery, Generation, Digestion, and Execution.
- •
  Systematic Diagnosis. Our analysis reveals distinct capability
  profiles hidden by answer accuracy, substantial latent execution
  capacity unlocked by correct primitives, and independent Discovery as
  the dominant bottleneck in mathematical reasoning. We further show
  that discovery-limited failures are substantially more amenable to
  post-training.
- •
  Internalizing primitive-guided reasoning. Building on these findings,
  we introduce Absorb, a primitive-privileged post-training paradigm
  that selectively transfers primitive-guided reasoning into the student
  model. Across multiple model scales and challenging mathematical
  reasoning benchmarks, Absorb consistently improves average performance
  by $`2.42`$ – $`4.48`$ points.

## 2 Mathematical Primitives as Structural Understanding

Rather than viewing mathematical problem solving as a sequence of steps,
we separate structural mathematical understanding from procedural
execution. We formalize the distinction through the Mathematical
Primitive
(§[2.1](#S2.SS1 "2.1 Mathematical Primitive ‣ 2 Mathematical Primitives as Structural Understanding ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models"))
and introduce Prim, a benchmark that evaluates LLM mathematical
reasoning across four dimensions: Generation, Discovery, Digestion, and
Execution
(§[2.3](#S2.SS3 "2.3 The Prim Benchmark ‣ 2 Mathematical Primitives as Structural Understanding ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models")).

### 2.1 Mathematical Primitive

A mathematical solution often begins before the first line of a proof,
when an opaque problem is recognized through the structure that makes it
solvable. We term this load-bearing structural understanding the
Mathematical Primitive
(Definition [1](#Thmtheorem1 "Definition 1 (Mathematical Primitive). ‣ 2.1 Mathematical Primitive ‣ 2 Mathematical Primitives as Structural Understanding ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models")).
Unlike generic advice such as use “induction” or “apply a theorem”, a
primitive identifies the structural property that makes such a strategy
applicable. It therefore serves as an intermediate reasoning object
between problem understanding and procedural solution construction.

###### Definition 1 (Mathematical Primitive).

For a mathematical problem, a _primitive_ is the essential conceptual
observation that reveals _why_ the problem can be solved. It captures
the latent mathematical structure shared by the problem and its
solution, such as an invariant, a theorem condition, a representation, a
reduction, or a reformulation. A primitive should be _concise_,
_problem-specific_, and _explanatory_: it must make clear what property
is being exploited and how that property unlocks the solution. It is
_not_ a routine calculation, a piece of generic advice, or a full proof.

### 2.2 Four Dimensions of Mathematical Understanding

Taking the mathematical primitive as the fundamental concept of
structural understanding, we systematically decompose mathematical
reasoning into four complementary dimensions. Let $`x`$ denote the input
problem, $`p`$ the corresponding mathematical primitive, $`y`$ a
complete proof or solution, and $`\pi`$ an LLM solver. The four
dimensions are defined as follows:

- •
  Discovery ($`\pi(x)\rightarrow\hat{p}`$) measures whether the model
  can independently identify the load-bearing mathematical primitive
  from the input problem alone.
- •
  Generation ($`\pi(x)\rightarrow\hat{y}`$) evaluates whether the model
  can solve the problem directly under zero-shot CoT prompting, with
  performance measured by exact match on the final answer.
- •
  Digestion ($`\pi(x,y)\rightarrow\hat{p}`$) instead provides the model
  with a complete correct solution and asks it to extract the
  mathematical primitive underlying the derivation, measuring whether
  the model can identify the underlying structure once a valid reasoning
  trajectory is exposed.
- •
  Execution ($`\pi(x,p)\rightarrow\hat{y}`$) conditions the solver on
  the mathematical primitive and evaluates whether it can successfully
  solve the problem once the relevant structure is explicitly provided.

Both Discovery and Digestion are evaluated using the scoring protocol
introduced in
§ [2.3](#S2.SS3 "2.3 The Prim Benchmark ‣ 2 Mathematical Primitives as Structural Understanding ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models").

### 2.3 The Prim Benchmark

Data Curation. We build on Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE) ([Center for AI
Safety et al., 2026](#bib.bib1)), focusing on its mathematics,
text-only, free-form subset with exactMatch evaluation. To reduce
annotation noise in the original benchmark, we draw from the
HLE-Verified release ([Zhai et al., 2026](#bib.bib2)), retaining its
_Gold_ and _Revision_ subsets, from which we randomly sample $`200`$
problems. For each problem, GPT-5.4-High generates an initial primitive
annotation conditioned on the problem, reference answer, and gold
rationale, following
Definition [1](#Thmtheorem1 "Definition 1 (Mathematical Primitive). ‣ 2.1 Mathematical Primitive ‣ 2 Mathematical Primitives as Structural Understanding ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models").
Three human experts with graduate-level training in mathematics
independently review the primitive and verify the validity of the
problem, answer, and rationale. This process excludes $`18`$ unsuitable
problems, yielding a final evaluation set of $`182`$. Further curation
and annotation details are provided in
Appendix [A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Dataset Filtering and Correction ‣ Appendix A Data Curation Details ‣ 6 Conclusion ‣ On-Policy Self-Distillation. ‣ 5 Related Work ‣ 4.4 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models").

Primitive Scoring. We evaluate each predicted primitive against the
human-annotated gold primitive, using the reference solution only to
recognize mathematically equivalent formulations. To account for
different forms of mathematical structure, each problem is assigned to
one of three primitive families, including Recast, Witness, and
Argument, with full definitions provided in
Appendix [A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Primitive Type and Family ‣ Appendix A Data Curation Details ‣ 6 Conclusion ‣ On-Policy Self-Distillation. ‣ 5 Related Work ‣ 4.4 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models").

Our scoring rubric evaluates three aspects of a predicted primitive:
$`V`$ determines whether the response constitutes a valid primitive,
$`\sigma_{\text{gate}}`$ measures whether it identifies the essential
mathematical structure, and $`\sigma_{\text{mech}}`$ measures whether it
explains how that structure enables the solution. We define

|     |                                                                                                                                                                                     |     |
| --- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{Score}=V\cdot\sigma_{\text{gate}}\cdot\big(0.6+0.4\cdot\sigma_{\text{mech}}\big),\quad\mathrm{PrimitiveAcc}=\mathbf{1}\left[\mathrm{Score}\geq\tau\right],`$ |     |

with $`\tau=0.8`$. This formulation treats validity and structural
identification as necessary conditions, while using mechanism quality to
refine the score. Further details are provided in
Appendix [A.3](#A1.SS3 "A.3 Primitive Scoring Protocol ‣ Appendix A Data Curation Details ‣ 6 Conclusion ‣ On-Policy Self-Distillation. ‣ 5 Related Work ‣ 4.4 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models").

## 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning

In this section, we conduct an empirical study of a diverse set of LLMs,
including both open- and closed-source models, on Prim. Moving beyond
standard answer correctness, our evaluation systematically disentangles
procedural execution from structural understanding. We report model
performance across four dimensions: Generation, Discovery, Digestion,
and Execution, following the evaluation protocol described in
§ [2.3](#S2.SS3 "2.3 The Prim Benchmark ‣ 2 Mathematical Primitives as Structural Understanding ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models").
The main results are summarized in
Table [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models").

We evaluate 12 models spanning three lineages and a broad capability
range. The OpenAI lineage includes the closed-source GPT-5.4 ([OpenAI,
2026b](#bib.bib3)), GPT-5.4-Mini ([OpenAI, 2026a](#bib.bib4)), and
GPT-5.4-Nano ([OpenAI, 2026a](#bib.bib4)), alongside the open-weight
GPT-OSS-20B ([OpenAI, 2025](#bib.bib5)). The Qwen lineage comprises
Qwen-3.6-27B ([Qwen Team, 2026b](#bib.bib6)) and Qwen-3.5-{27B, 9B,
4B} ([Qwen Team, 2026a](#bib.bib7)). The DeepSeek lineage features
DeepSeek-R1-0528-Qwen3-8B ([DeepSeek-AI, 2025](#bib.bib8)) and
DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-{32B, 14B, 7B} ([DeepSeek-AI,
2025](#bib.bib8)). We use high reasoning effort when available and a
maximum generation budget of 120k tokens per problem.

### 3.2 Results Analysis

Table [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models")
presents the comprehensive evaluation results of all models on Prim.
Performance in the Discovery and Digestion dimensions is assessed by the
model’s capacity to isolate the underlying mathematical primitive,
utilizing the scoring protocol detailed in
§ [2.3](#S2.SS3 "2.3 The Prim Benchmark ‣ 2 Mathematical Primitives as Structural Understanding ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models").
Meanwhile, Generation and Execution are evaluated based on standard
final-answer accuracy, following the HLE benchmark ([Center for AI
Safety et al., 2026](#bib.bib1)). Further details on the diagnostic
evaluation and additional analyses are provided in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Additional Details on Diagnostic Evaluation ‣ 6 Conclusion ‣ On-Policy Self-Distillation. ‣ 5 Related Work ‣ 4.4 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models").

![Refer to caption](2610.02191v1/figs/s-d-composition.png)

Figure 2: Joint composition of Generation and Discovery outcomes across
models.

Finding 1: Answer accuracy masks distinct capability profiles.
Final-answer accuracy conflates structural discovery with downstream
execution. As shown in
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models"),
Discovery and Generation are positively associated overall, yet models
with similar solving accuracy can exhibit sharply different structural
capabilities. For example, Qwen3.6-27B and gpt-5.4-mini achieve
comparable Generation performance, while differing by over $`30`$
percentage points in Discovery. Conversely, GPT-5.4 achieves
substantially higher Discovery than Generation. The problem-level
decomposition in
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models")
reveals similarly distinct profiles across model families. The OpenAI
lineage is more primitive-forward, with successful Generation frequently
accompanied by correct Discovery and a substantial fraction of cases
with correct Discovery but failed Generation ($`D^{+}G^{-}`$). In
contrast, Qwen exhibits more cases with failed Discovery but successful
Generation ($`D^{-}G^{+}`$), despite competitive Generation performance.
The DeepSeek-R1 distilled models are more heavily concentrated in joint
Discovery–Generation failures. Thus, similar top-line accuracy can arise
from markedly different underlying capability profiles.

![Refer to
caption](2610.02191v1/figs/discovery_vs_generation_y_equals.png)

Figure 3: Discovery versus Generation across all evaluated models on
Prim.

Qualitative analysis further clarifies these asymmetries. For gpt-5.4,
$`D^{+}G^{-}`$ cases primarily reflect two post-primitive failure modes:
❶ technical knowledge gaps, where the correct structure is identified
but a required lemma, theorem condition, or domain-specific fact is
missing; and ❷ procedural execution failures, such as algebraic errors,
missed edge cases, or unresolved logical gaps. For Qwen3.6-27B, among
$`D^{-}G^{+}`$ cases, the decisive structural idea often emerges after
an initial attempt without using it, typically around one quarter into
the reasoning trace; in most remaining cases it appears at the outset,
and only rarely is it absent entirely. The corresponding cold Discovery
output often captures a partial form of the correct idea but misses its
decisive component. Together with the longer reasoning traces in
Figure [12](#A2.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ B.3.2 Reasoning Length and Generation Behavior ‣ B.3.1 Performance across Primitive Families ‣ B.3 Additional Experiment Results ‣ Appendix B Additional Details on Diagnostic Evaluation ‣ 6 Conclusion ‣ On-Policy Self-Distillation. ‣ 5 Related Work ‣ 4.4 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models"),
this pattern is consistent with a more grind-first profile, where the
relevant structure tends to emerge during extended procedural
exploration rather than being isolated before execution.

Finding 2: Correct primitives unlock latent execution capacity. To
examine whether models possess downstream capabilities that are not
realized during direct Generation, we evaluate Execution when the
correct Mathematical Primitive is explicitly provided. As shown in
Table [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models"),
primitive guidance improves performance by $`17.58`$ to $`29.67`$
percentage points across all 12 models. Notably, under the same
primitive-guided setting, the Qwen models achieve Execution performance
competitive with the closed-source gpt-5.4 variants despite
substantially weaker Discovery. This gap shows that difficulty
independently identifying the relevant mathematical structure can
coexist with strong downstream problem-solving capability once that
structure is available. More broadly, these gains indicate that many
Generation failures mask downstream solving capacity that models can
successfully exercise when the relevant mathematical structure is
supplied.

| ------------ | ---------- | ------------------------ | ----------------- | ------------------ | ------------------ |
| Model        | Generation | Execution                |                   |                    |                    |
|              |            | Self-Generated Primitive | Teacher Plan      | Teacher Primitive  | Gold Primitive     |
| gpt-5.4-mini | $`50.55`$  | $`48.90`$ (-1.65)        | $`60.44`$ (+9.89) | $`63.74`$ (+13.19) | $`71.98`$ (+21.43) |
| gpt-5.4-nano | $`44.51`$  | $`46.15`$ (+1.64)        | $`54.40`$ (+9.89) | $`60.99`$ (+16.48) | $`68.68`$ (+24.17) |
| Qwen3.6-27B  | $`52.75`$  | $`41.21`$ (-11.54)       | $`56.04`$ (+3.29) | $`64.84`$ (+12.09) | $`78.57`$ (+25.82) |

Table 2: Generation and Execution performance on Prim under different
forms of reasoning support. Detailed results are presented in Table
[B.3.3](#A2.SS3.SSS3 "B.3.3 Execution under Different Primitive Sources ‣ B.3.2 Reasoning Length and Generation Behavior ‣ B.3.1 Performance across Primitive Families ‣ B.3 Additional Experiment Results ‣ Appendix B Additional Details on Diagnostic Evaluation ‣ 6 Conclusion ‣ On-Policy Self-Distillation. ‣ 5 Related Work ‣ 4.4 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models")
in Appendix
[B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Additional Experiment Results ‣ Appendix B Additional Details on Diagnostic Evaluation ‣ 6 Conclusion ‣ On-Policy Self-Distillation. ‣ 5 Related Work ‣ 4.4 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models").

We further investigate whether this rescue can be attributed simply to
task decomposition or generic procedural scaffolding.
Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models")
compares four intervention settings. Conditioning the model on its own
generated primitive provides little benefit: it yields only a marginal
gain for gpt-5.4-nano and substantially degrades Qwen3.6-27B, indicating
that a forced discover-then-execute decomposition alone is insufficient.
We then compare two forms of external guidance generated by the same
teacher model (gpt-5.4) from the problem alone: a step-by-step Teacher
Plan, which serves as a procedural hint by specifying the major solution
steps, and a Teacher Primitive, which is generated according to the
definition of primitive. Although the Teacher Plan improves over direct
Generation, the Teacher Primitive yields substantially larger gains
across the evaluated models. The Gold Primitive further maximizes this
effect, pushing accuracy to $`71.98\%`$, $`68.68\%`$, and $`78.57\%`$
for the representative models. This contrast provides crucial empirical
validation for our premise in
§[2.1](#S2.SS1 "2.1 Mathematical Primitive ‣ 2 Mathematical Primitives as Structural Understanding ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models"):
a mathematical primitive is fundamentally distinct from, and vastly more
effective than, a generic plan or hint. The rescue effect therefore
cannot be attributed to task decomposition or the procedural scaffold
evaluated here alone; exposing the load-bearing mathematical structure
provides a substantially stronger signal for downstream reasoning.

Finding 3: Independent structural discovery is the dominant bottleneck.
As shown in
Table [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models"),
models perform substantially better on Digestion, recovering the
Mathematical Primitive from a correct solution, than on Discovery, where
the same primitive must be identified from the problem alone. This
asymmetry is particularly pronounced outside the strongest OpenAI
models. Even models with weak Discovery can often recover the organizing
primitive once the relevant reasoning is exposed through a completed
solution; for instance, Qwen3.6-27B rises from 24.73% Discovery to
92.31% Digestion and R1-Distill-32B from 6.04% to 65.38%.

![Refer to caption](2610.02191v1/figs/faliure_mode_decomposition.png)

Figure 4: Decomposition of Generation failures by Discovery ($`D`$) and
Execution ($`E`$). Detailed results can be found in
Table [B.3.3](#A2.SS3.SSS3 "B.3.3 Execution under Different Primitive Sources ‣ B.3.2 Reasoning Length and Generation Behavior ‣ B.3.1 Performance across Primitive Families ‣ B.3 Additional Experiment Results ‣ Appendix B Additional Details on Diagnostic Evaluation ‣ 6 Conclusion ‣ On-Policy Self-Distillation. ‣ 5 Related Work ‣ 4.4 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models")
in
Appendix [B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Additional Experiment Results ‣ Appendix B Additional Details on Diagnostic Evaluation ‣ 6 Conclusion ‣ On-Policy Self-Distillation. ‣ 5 Related Work ‣ 4.4 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models").

These results reveal a pronounced gap between retrospective recognition
and prospective discovery of mathematical structure: models can often
recognize the key idea once it is instantiated in a valid solution, yet
struggle to identify it independently before the derivation is known.

To further localize this bottleneck, we decompose Generation failures
according to the joint outcomes of Discovery ($`D`$) and Execution
($`E`$), as shown in
Figure [4](#S3.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models").
A striking $`83.6\%`$ of all failures fall into the $`D^{-}`$ regime,
indicating that failed primitive discovery dominates the failure
landscape. Importantly, a substantial fraction of these cases are
discovery-limited failures ($`D^{-}E^{+}`$): the model fails to identify
the correct primitive independently, yet succeeds once it is supplied.
This reveals that, for many failures, latent execution capacity is
already present but remains inaccessible because of the upstream
bottleneck in primitive discovery.

### 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable?

While our preceding diagnosis reveals the failure modes of LLMs during
inference, a natural follow-up question arises: how does post-training
impact these mathematical reasoning failures? Of particular interest are
discovery-limited failures, which exhibit substantial room for
improvement
(§[3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models")).
We hypothesize that these failures lie just at the boundary of the
models’ reasoning capabilities, making them highly amenable to repair
through post-training. Therefore, we utilize Supervised Fine-Tuning
(SFT) and On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) ([Zhao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib19)) to investigate how different failure modes uniquely
respond to these post-training paradigms.

Setup. Our training corpus contains 709 Mathematics Ph.D.
qualifying-examination problems from 1991–2026, each paired with a
human-authored proof (median length: 118 words); additional details are
provided in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Post-Training Dataset Details ‣ B.3.5 Repairability across Failure Modes ‣ B.3.4 Failure Decomposition and Rescue Analysis ‣ B.3.3 Execution under Different Primitive Sources ‣ B.3.2 Reasoning Length and Generation Behavior ‣ B.3.1 Performance across Primitive Families ‣ B.3 Additional Experiment Results ‣ Appendix B Additional Details on Diagnostic Evaluation ‣ 6 Conclusion ‣ On-Policy Self-Distillation. ‣ 5 Related Work ‣ 4.4 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models").
We use qualifying-examination problems because their open-ended,
proof-oriented nature closely matches the difficulty and structural
reasoning demands of Prim. Since such problems generally lack
algorithmically verifiable short answers, we focus on text-supervised
post-training rather than outcome-verified methods such as RLVR. We
evaluate SFT and OPSD on Qwen-3.5-27B, 9B, 4B ([Qwen Team,
2026a](#bib.bib7)), using the default OPSD configuration, bfloat16
precision, a fixed seed of $`42`$, and NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada GPUs.

On-Policy Self-Distillation. Given training examples $`\{x,y\}`$, where
$`x`$ denotes the input problem and $`y`$ its reference solution, both
the teacher and student policies are initialized from the same base
model $`\pi_{0}`$. At each decoding step $`t`$, the student
autoregressively generates an on-policy response, inducing the token
distribution $`P_{t}:=\pi_{S}(\cdot\mid\hat{y}_{<t},x)`$, while the
teacher distribution $`Q_{t}:=\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid\hat{y}_{<t},x,y)`$
additionally conditions on the reference solution. Notably, both
policies are conditioned on the same student prefix $`\hat{y}_{<t}`$,
allowing the teacher to provide token-level supervision along the
student’s own reasoning trajectory. OPSD minimizes the divergence
between these distributions:

|     |                                                                                                                                                                                                  |     |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPSD}}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}D(P_{t},Q_{t})=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}D\left(\pi_{S}(\cdot\mid\hat{y}_{<t},x),\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid\hat{y}_{<t},x,y)\right),`$ |     |

where $`D`$ is instantiated as Kullback–Leibler (KL), reverse KL (rKL),
or Jensen–Shannon (JSD). Specifically, KL uses
$`D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q_{t}\parallel P_{t})`$, rKL uses
$`D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{t}\parallel Q_{t})`$, and JSD is symmetric in
$`P_{t}`$ and $`Q_{t}`$.

Results. Across the 27B, 9B, and 4B models, the base models leave
$`341`$ failure instances in Prim. We focus on the $`294`$ cases with
failed Discovery: $`147`$ $`D^{-}E^{+}`$ and $`147`$ $`D^{-}E^{-}`$
cases. We define repair as an incorrect baseline Generation response
becoming correct after post-training. As shown in
Table [3](#S3.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models"),
SFT and OPSD repair $`20.4\%`$ and $`21.1\%`$ of $`D^{-}E^{+}`$ cases,
roughly three

|                |       |       |
| -------------- | ----- | ----- |
| Failure type   | SFT   | OPSD  |
| $`D^{-}E^{+}`$ | 20.4% | 21.1% |
| $`D^{-}E^{-}`$ | 6.8%  | 8.2%  |

Table 3: Post-training repair rates of SFT and OPSD across initial Prim
failure quadrants.

times their respective rates of $`6.8\%`$ and $`8.2\%`$ for
$`D^{-}E^{-}`$ cases. This ordering holds at each model scale,
identifying discovery-limited failures as a promising target for
post-training. However, net gains in Generation remain modest (as shown
in
Table [4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 4.2 Bounded Override ‣ 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models"))
because some initially correct cases become incorrect, offsetting part
of these repairs. These regressions are consistent with post-training
drift and suggest that supervision from reference proofs should be
transferred more selectively.

## 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning

In this section, we introduce Absorb, a novel variant of on-policy
self-distillation that improves the mathematical problem-solving
capability of LLMs by internalizing primitive-guided reasoning,
motivated by the observations in
§[3](#S3 "3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models").
Extensive experiments with Qwen models as backbones show that Absorb
consistently outperforms strong baselines on a diverse set of
mathematical reasoning benchmarks
(§[4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models")).
Further implementation details and ablation results are provided in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Post-Training Ablation Studies ‣ B.3.5 Repairability across Failure Modes ‣ B.3.4 Failure Decomposition and Rescue Analysis ‣ B.3.3 Execution under Different Primitive Sources ‣ B.3.2 Reasoning Length and Generation Behavior ‣ B.3.1 Performance across Primitive Families ‣ B.3 Additional Experiment Results ‣ Appendix B Additional Details on Diagnostic Evaluation ‣ 6 Conclusion ‣ On-Policy Self-Distillation. ‣ 5 Related Work ‣ 4.4 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models").

### 4.1 Primitives as Privileged Information

![Refer to caption](2610.02191v1/ipsd_illustration_wrap.png)

Figure 5: Illustration of Absorb paradigm.

Our diagnosis in
§[3](#S3 "3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models")
identifies missing mathematical primitives as the primary bottleneck in
discovery-limited problems. A natural remedy is to directly supervise
primitive generation. In practice, however, this objective transfers
poorly to solution reasoning, likely reflecting a mismatch between
structural understanding and step-by-step generation, as further
supported by the ablations in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Post-Training Ablation Studies ‣ B.3.5 Repairability across Failure Modes ‣ B.3.4 Failure Decomposition and Rescue Analysis ‣ B.3.3 Execution under Different Primitive Sources ‣ B.3.2 Reasoning Length and Generation Behavior ‣ B.3.1 Performance across Primitive Families ‣ B.3 Additional Experiment Results ‣ Appendix B Additional Details on Diagnostic Evaluation ‣ 6 Conclusion ‣ On-Policy Self-Distillation. ‣ 5 Related Work ‣ 4.4 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models").
More importantly,
§[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models")
shows that post-training can repair discovery-limited failures while
leaving Discovery largely unchanged. This dissociation suggests that
effective reasoning does not require primitives to be explicitly
generated; instead, they can guide the reasoning trajectory implicitly.

Motivated by this observation, we provide mathematical primitives as
privileged information to the teacher rather than as prediction targets
for the student. This mirrors our Execution evaluation, where providing
the primitive unlocks latent execution capability, and uses the same
primitive-conditioned reasoning to guide post-training. Compared with
full reference proofs, primitives provide more targeted supervision by
supplying the missing structural information without prescribing
execution steps the student can already perform. This design transfers
primitive-guided reasoning into the student’s own generation process
without requiring primitives at inference time.

### 4.2 Bounded Override

Given the reasoning drift observed with existing post-training methods,
indiscriminate teacher intervention should be avoided. Moreover,
introducing mathematical primitives as privileged information can cause
substantial privilege leakage under naive OPSD on complex reasoning
problems, as shown in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Post-Training Ablation Studies ‣ B.3.5 Repairability across Failure Modes ‣ B.3.4 Failure Decomposition and Rescue Analysis ‣ B.3.3 Execution under Different Primitive Sources ‣ B.3.2 Reasoning Length and Generation Behavior ‣ B.3.1 Performance across Primitive Families ‣ B.3 Additional Experiment Results ‣ Appendix B Additional Details on Diagnostic Evaluation ‣ 6 Conclusion ‣ On-Policy Self-Distillation. ‣ 5 Related Work ‣ 4.4 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models").
This motivates a selective transfer mechanism that preserves useful
privileged guidance while limiting how strongly it can override the
student’s own reasoning. Intuitively, the teacher should pull the
student toward better choices without abruptly displacing preferences
that the student has already formed. The primitive should refine the
student’s existing reasoning space rather than force it to imitate
decisions that are only accessible under privileged context.

This leads to two design principles: ❶ when the privileged teacher
assigns higher preference to a choice than the student, this positive
guidance should be transferred in full, as it directly reflects
information contributed by the primitive; and ❷ when the teacher
strongly suppresses a choice favored by the student, the resulting
pressure should be bounded, since large disagreement may arise from
privileged information unavailable to the student rather than from an
error it can independently recognize. Importantly, bounding this
negative pressure does not freeze incorrect student preferences:
positive guidance toward better alternatives remains fully active,
progressively shifting probability mass away from suboptimal choices
over training. These desiderata admit a simple implementation through
reverse KL with one-sided clamping, which preserves positive teacher
guidance while bounding excessive suppression of student-preferred
choices.

### 4.3 Overall Objective

Combining the two design principles above, we introduce Absorb,
illustrated in
Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.1 Primitives as Privileged Information ‣ 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models").
Absorb conditions the teacher on the mathematical primitive $`p`$ to
provide targeted guidance for the missing discovery signal, while
bounding how strongly this can override the student’s own reasoning. Let
$`\mathcal{S}_{t}`$ denote the teacher’s top-$`K`$ token support at step
$`t`$, and let $`\bar{\pi}_{S}`$ and $`\bar{\pi}_{T}`$ denote the
student and privileged-teacher distributions renormalized over
$`\mathcal{S}_{t}`$, respectively. The resulting objective is:

|     |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |     |
| --- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\textsc{Absorb}{}}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{v\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}\min\left\{\bar{\pi}_{S}(v\mid\hat{y}_{<t},x)\log\frac{\bar{\pi}_{S}(v\mid\hat{y}_{<t},x)}{\bar{\pi}_{T}(v\mid\hat{y}_{<t},x,p)},\tau\right\}.`$ |     |

Here, the privileged teacher injects primitive-guided information along
the student’s on-policy reasoning trajectory, while the one-sided clamp
preserves its positive guidance toward better alternatives and bounds
excessive suppression of choices favored by the student.

### 4.4 Experimental Results

Setup. For implementing Absorb, we utilize the identical base models and
optimization configurations detailed in
§[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models"),
differing only in the substitution of the standard OPSD objective with
our primitive-privileged divergence loss
($`\mathcal{L}_{\text{ABSORB}}`$). To comprehensively evaluate
internalized reasoning capabilities and generalization, we assess
performance across four challenging mathematical benchmarks: our curated
Prim (evaluating both Generation and Discovery), the full mathematics
subset of HLE-Verified ([Zhai et al., 2026](#bib.bib2)),
HMMT25 ([Dekoninck et al., 2026](#bib.bib20)), and Omni-MATH ([Gao et
al., 2025](#bib.bib21)). To account for the extreme difficulty of the
competition-level datasets, we report pass@4 accuracy for HMMT25 and
Omni-MATH. The overall average (Avg.) is computed exclusively over the
Generation scores across all four benchmarks, excluding Discovery.

Results. As shown in
Table [4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 4.2 Bounded Override ‣ 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models"),
Absorb consistently outperforms SFT and OPSD across model scales and
benchmarks. At the 9B scale, SFT and OPSD reduce Generation accuracy by
$`6.04`$ and $`4.95`$ percentage points, respectively, while OPSD incurs
a $`3.30`$-point drop at the 27B scale. These regressions explain the
modest net gains discussed in
§[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models"):
repairing previously failed problems can be offset by newly introduced
errors on problems the model already solves. In contrast, Absorb
improves Generation at all three model scales, including a $`5.49`$
point gain at 9B and a $`3.73`$ point improvement in average benchmark
performance. This pattern is consistent with the role of bounded
override: selective transfer retains useful primitive-guided information
while limiting disruptive changes to the model’s existing reasoning
behavior. The results also support the intended internalization of
primitive-guided reasoning. Improvements from Absorb are concentrated in
downstream reasoning rather than explicit Discovery. At the 9B scale,
Generation improves by $`5.49`$ points while Discovery increases by only
$`1.10`$; at 27B, Generation improves by $`1.10`$ points and HLE Math by
$`3.93`$, despite a $`0.55`$-point decrease in Discovery. Thus, the
benefit of the primitive need not manifest as better explicit primitive
recovery; instead, its structural guidance is increasingly reflected in
the model’s unassisted reasoning process.

## 5 Related Work

##### Mathematical Reasoning in LLMs.

Mathematical reasoning benchmarks have rapidly escalated in difficulty,
progressing from early grade-school and competition datasets (e.g.,
MathQA ([Amini et al., 2019](#bib.bib38)), ASDiv ([Miao et al.,
2020](#bib.bib39)), SVAMP ([Patel et al., 2021](#bib.bib40)),
GSM8K ([Cobbe et al., 2021](#bib.bib31)), MATH ([Hendrycks et al.,
2021](#bib.bib32))) to advanced Olympiad- and expert-level frontiers
(TheoremQA ([Chen et al., 2023](#bib.bib41)), MathBench ([Liu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib42)), AIME ([Dekoninck et al., 2026](#bib.bib20)),
OlympiadBench ([He et al., 2024](#bib.bib33)), Omni-MATH ([Gao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib21)), HLE ([Center for AI Safety et al.,
2026](#bib.bib1)), FrontierMath ([Glazer et al., 2024](#bib.bib34))).
Despite this scaling in complexity, evaluation predominantly remains
rigidly anchored to final-answer correctness. Recognizing the
limitations of outcome-based metrics, recent literature explores
process-oriented evaluation: SMART ([Hou et al., 2026](#bib.bib35))
decomposes problem-solving across cognitive dimensions,
ReasoningMath-Plus ([Zheng et al., 2026](#bib.bib36)) verifies minimal
procedural skeletons, and DeepInsightTheorem ([Li et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib37)) leverages proof sketches for intermediate
supervision. Executable Functional Abstractions (EFAs) ([Khan et al.,
2025](#bib.bib43)) represent mathematical structure as executable
generative programs, whereas our Mathematical Primitive captures the
concise, non-procedural idea underlying a specific solution. Our
approach instead isolates the load-bearing _mathematical primitive_,
decoupling structural understanding from procedural execution. We
evaluate whether models can discover it from a problem, recover it from
a solution, and execute the proof when it is provided.

##### On-Policy Self-Distillation.

On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) advances knowledge distillation for
LLM reasoning by mitigating the distribution shift inherent in
traditional off-policy methods ([Zhao et al., 2026](#bib.bib19); [He et
al., 2026](#bib.bib23); [Penaloza et al., 2026](#bib.bib25)).
Specifically, the student generates its own reasoning trajectories
on-policy, while the teacher, conditioned on additional privileged
information, provides dense supervision along these rollouts, with both
sharing the same base model. However, recent studies show that naive
OPSD can suffer from privilege leakage and suppress exploratory or
self-corrective reasoning. To address this, [Shen et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib22) isolate inference-transferable supervision from
reference-induced shortcuts, while [Kaur et al. (2026)](#bib.bib24);
[Peng et al. (2026)](#bib.bib29) focus on preserving high-entropy
decision points and epistemic behaviors from aggressive
privileged-teacher corrections. Other approaches modulate supervision
based on teacher–student disagreement ([Li et al., 2026b](#bib.bib28);
[Yu et al., 2026](#bib.bib27); [Xie et al., 2026](#bib.bib30)), or
utilize RL primarily for token-level credit assignment ([Yang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib26)). AVSD mitigates privilege leakage by separating
shared and view-specific signals across multiple privileged
views ([Nguyen et al., 2026](#bib.bib44)). Absorb differs primarily in
the privileged signal itself. Rather than conditioning the teacher on a
full solution, Absorb uses the primitive as privileged information and
selectively transfers its guidance through a bounded override mechanism.

## 6 Conclusion

In this paper, we introduced the notion of Mathematical Primitive and
Prim, a benchmark for systematically evaluating structural mathematical
understanding in LLMs across Discovery, Generation, Digestion, and
Execution. Our diagnosis reveals that similar solution accuracy can mask
markedly different capability profiles, correct primitives can unlock
substantial latent execution capacity, and independent Discovery
constitutes a dominant bottleneck in mathematical reasoning. We further
show that discovery-limited failures are substantially more amenable to
post-training, while existing methods can introduce regressions on
problems the model already solves. Building on these findings, we
proposed Absorb, a primitive-privileged post-training paradigm that
selectively transfers primitive-guided reasoning through a bounded
override mechanism. Experiments on challenging mathematical reasoning
benchmarks show that Absorb consistently improves over strong
post-training baselines. Overall, our results highlight the value of
explicitly diagnosing structural mathematical understanding and
leveraging this structure to improve LLM reasoning.

By systematically investigating mathematical understanding in LLMs, we
hope this work encourages a broader shift in AI for Science from
optimizing benchmark performance alone toward identifying the
capabilities required for scientific problem solving and discovery.
Given the foundational role of mathematics across STEM disciplines, this
structural perspective may extend beyond mathematics. We highlight three
promising directions. First, our diagnostic framework could be
generalized to other structurally rigorous domains, such as theoretical
physics and computational chemistry. Second, the observed
discovery-execution asymmetry suggests a potential design principle for
mathematical agents: explicitly separating structural search from
procedural execution may enable more effective allocation of
inference-time computation. Finally, future work could explore
integrating mathematical primitives with formal verification systems
such as Lean, connecting informal structural reasoning with formal proof
generation.

## Appendix A Data Curation Details

### A.1 Dataset Filtering and Correction

To reduce annotation noise in the original HLE, we draw from the
community-verified HLE-Verified release ([Zhai et al.,
2026](#bib.bib2)), retaining only its _Gold_ and _Revision_ subsets. We
randomly sample $`200`$ text-only problems and conduct an additional
expert review for primitive-level evaluation. This process excludes
$`18`$ unsuitable problems due to ill-posed or ambiguous questions,
incorrect or unverifiable answers, non-self-contained tasks,
insufficient rationales, exhaustive-computation requirements, or other
quality issues. For $`17`$ of these $`18`$ problems, no valid gold
primitive could be established, yielding a final benchmark of $`182`$
problems.

Expert review further identifies residual errors in the official answers
of $`15`$ retained problems, including $`13`$ mathematical errors and
$`2`$ corrupted answer strings, which we correct in our benchmark.
Re-evaluating the strongest model on these corrected answers flips
$`11`$ predictions from incorrect to correct, with no reverse flips,
providing an additional consistency check on the revisions.

Because gold primitives are derived with access to reference solutions,
we also audit them for answer leakage. We search the concatenated
primitive fields for bounded occurrences of the gold answer, using token
boundaries designed to avoid spurious numeral matches. This audit
initially identifies $`4`$ affected primitives. We manually revise them
to remove the leaked answers while preserving their structural content,
and verify that no direct answer-string leakage remains in the final
benchmark.

### A.2 Primitive Type and Family

To make the definition operational and to structure evaluation, we
anchor every primitive to a frozen taxonomy of ten primitive _types_
(plus a computation_only escape hatch for problems that genuinely have
no kernel primitive in the sense of
Definition [1](#Thmtheorem1 "Definition 1 (Mathematical Primitive). ‣ 2.1 Mathematical Primitive ‣ 2 Mathematical Primitives as Structural Understanding ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models")),
as presented in
Table [5](#A1.T5 "Table 5 ‣ A.2 Primitive Type and Family ‣ Appendix A Data Curation Details ‣ 6 Conclusion ‣ On-Policy Self-Distillation. ‣ 5 Related Work ‣ 4.4 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models").

|                              |                                                                              |
| ---------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Type                         | The essential property is…                                                   |
| reformulation                | a change of language/encoding/viewpoint makes the problem tractable          |
| hidden_structure             | the objects secretly carry a known structure (group, graph, metric space, …) |
| invariant_or_monotonicity    | a preserved or monotone quantity constrains all transformations              |
| theorem_applicability        | the task reduces to verifying the hypotheses of a known theorem              |
| duality_or_representation    | a dual / spectral / transformed viewpoint simplifies the problem             |
| extremal_principle           | a maximal/minimal/extreme object forces structure                            |
| construction_or_witness      | an explicit object/certificate/counterexample is built                       |
| reduction_or_embedding       | the problem is reduced/embedded into a known canonical one                   |
| obstruction_or_contradiction | the opposite assumption violates a necessary constraint                      |
| induction_or_recursion       | a recursive/self-similar structure with a strengthened hypothesis            |

Table 5: The ten primitive types.

|          |                                                                                                           |                                                                                                     |                                                                              |
| -------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Family   | Routed primitive types                                                                                    | Gate (what)                                                                                         | Mechanism (how)                                                              |
| Recast   | reformulation, hidden_structure, reduction_or_embedding, duality_or_representation, theorem_applicability | target setting $`Y`$ (equivalent form / hidden structure / canonical target / dual / named theorem) | how $`Y`$ unlocks it; for theorems, hypotheses verified                      |
| Witness  | construction_or_witness, extremal_principle, invariant_or_monotonicity                                    | the object (construction / certificate / extremal / invariant–monotone)                             | its decisive property: built to satisfy / extremality / invariance forces it |
| Argument | obstruction_or_contradiction, induction_or_recursion                                                      | the load-bearing claim (specific obstruction / strengthened hypothesis)                             | why the opposite fails / how the recursion closes                            |

Table 6: The primitive families. Each of the ten frozen primitive types
routes to exactly one family.

Further, since the same problem can often be solved through conceptually
different routes, we further assign the primary primitive type as
presented in
Table [6](#A1.T6 "Table 6 ‣ A.2 Primitive Type and Family ‣ Appendix A Data Curation Details ‣ 6 Conclusion ‣ On-Policy Self-Distillation. ‣ 5 Related Work ‣ 4.4 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models")
of each problem to one of three _families_: Recast, Witness, or
Argument, as summarized below:

- •
  Recast: The load-bearing object is the _target setting_ $`Y`$ into
  which the original problem is moved, such as an equivalent
  reformulation, a hidden known structure, a canonical target problem, a
  dual or representational viewpoint, or a named theorem. The gate asks
  whether the model recasts the problem into the same $`Y`$, or a
  provably equivalent one up to trivial restatement. The mechanism asks
  how this target setting unlocks the solution, such as the reduction
  step actually used, or, in theorem-based cases, whether the theorem’s
  hypotheses are correctly verified. Moving to a different setting,
  naming the wrong theorem, or remaining entirely within the original
  framing constitutes a gate mismatch; identifying a coarser or weaker
  target receives partial credit.
- •
  Witness: The load-bearing object is a specific mathematical _object_:
  a construction, certificate, witness, extremal object, invariant, or
  monotone quantity. The gate asks whether the model identifies the same
  object, or an equivalent object that plays the identical role in the
  solution. The mechanism asks for its decisive property: for example,
  why the construction satisfies the required constraint, why
  extremality forces the conclusion, or why invariance forbids or forces
  the desired outcome. An object of the correct general kind but without
  the decisive feature receives partial credit, such as a
  near-construction that fails the needed property or a monotone
  quantity that is not the one driving the proof.
- •
  Argument: The load-bearing object is the central _claim_ on which the
  proof depends, such as the obstruction contradicted by the opposite
  assumption or the strengthened induction hypothesis needed for the
  recursive step. The gate asks whether the model’s reasoning hinges on
  the same claim; merely naming the proof style, such as “by
  contradiction” or “by induction”, is not sufficient. The mechanism
  asks for the logical step itself, such as why the opposite assumption
  violates the constraint or how the strengthened hypothesis closes the
  induction. Stating only the proof style without the specific
  load-bearing claim is a gate mismatch, while a related but loosely
  stated or under-strengthened claim receives partial credit.

### A.3 Primitive Scoring Protocol

Mathematical primitive correctness is evaluated against the annotated
_gold primitive_, with the problem’s full reference solution
(_rationale_) supplied as supporting context. The rationale is provided
only so the judge can recognize coarser phrasings, equivalent
paraphrases, or alternative routes that the reference solution shows to
be valid, i.e. so a correct primitive is not penalized merely for
failing to match the terse gold annotation verbatim, while never
requiring the model to reproduce the downstream execution.

All three primitive families share the same three-verdict decomposition
$`(V,\sigma_{\text{gate}},\sigma_{\text{mech}})`$ and the deterministic
scoring rule in
§ [2.3](#S2.SS3 "2.3 The Prim Benchmark ‣ 2 Mathematical Primitives as Structural Understanding ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models").
Here, $`V\in\{0,1\}`$ is a binary validity indicator (is the output a
genuine primitive rather than a generic remark, a bare technique name,
or pure computation), while the two graded slots
$`\sigma_{\text{gate}},\sigma_{\text{mech}}\in\{0,\tfrac{1}{2},1\}`$
evaluate whether the response identifies the essential what (the _gate_)
and explains the operative how (the _mechanism_). The difference across
families is the type of mathematical object over which these two slots
are instantiated, ensuring that “the same idea” is matched against the
appropriate target. Because $`V`$ is binary and
$`\sigma_{\text{gate}},\sigma_{\text{mech}}\in\{0,\tfrac{1}{2},1\}`$,
the score lies in $`[0,1]`$ but is restricted to the finite set, and we
have
$`\mathrm{Score}\in\{0,\;0.30,\;0.40,\;0.50,\;0.60,\;0.80,\;1.00\}.`$

All primitive judgments are produced by GPT-5.4-High at temperature 0.
To validate the judge, we sampled $`200`$ (model, problem) pairs,
$`100`$ judged primitive-correct and $`100`$ judged primitive-incorrect,
stratified across the $`12`$ evaluated models. Three annotators with
graduate-level mathematical training, blind to the judge’s verdict,
independently labeled $`\mathrm{PrimitiveAcc}`$. Judge–human agreement
is $`95.5\%`$ (Cohen’s $`\kappa=0.91`$), with $`9`$ disagreements.

Because each problem is scored against a single gold primitive, a
response following a genuinely different but valid conceptual route may
be under-credited. To assess this limitation, we further examined the
$`100`$ primitive-incorrect cases in the same validation sample
($`8`$–$`9`$ per model, fixed seed): exactly $`1`$ case ($`1\%`$)
contained a valid alternative primitive missed by the single-gold
rubric. We additionally audited all $`32`$ problems marked
primitive-incorrect for the strongest model (gpt-5.4,
$`\mathrm{Score}<0.8`$), identifying exactly $`1`$ such case. These
audits suggest that, although the single-gold rubric may conservatively
underestimate valid primitive generation, under-counting due to
alternative conceptual routes is rare in the audited cases.

### A.4 Illustrative Example of Mathematical Primitives

To make the notion of a mathematical primitive concrete, we provide a
representative example in
Figure [6](#A1.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ A.4 Illustrative Example of Mathematical Primitives ‣ Appendix A Data Curation Details ‣ 6 Conclusion ‣ On-Policy Self-Distillation. ‣ 5 Related Work ‣ 4.4 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models").
The full rationale contains the complete derivation needed to solve the
problem, whereas the primitive isolates the underlying structural idea
that makes the derivation possible. Due to space constraints, we show
only the core_concept field in the figure. This example illustrates that
a primitive is not a shortened proof, but a compact representation of
the key mathematical structure underlying the solution.

### A.5 Prompt on Extracting a Mathematical Primitive and Primitive Scoring

During data curation, we use a teacher model to extract a mathematical
primitive for each problem. As shown in
Figure [7](#A1.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ A.5 Prompt on Extracting a Mathematical Primitive and Primitive Scoring ‣ Appendix A Data Curation Details ‣ 6 Conclusion ‣ On-Policy Self-Distillation. ‣ 5 Related Work ‣ 4.4 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models"),
the teacher is asked to identify the essential mathematical property
underlying the problem and explain the solution principle enabled by
that property, while explicitly avoiding calculations or solution steps.
We additionally require a structured primitive classification, including
a primary type, optional secondary types, a classification rationale,
and a confidence score.

We evaluate each predicted primitive using three complementary signals.
First, the validity term $`V`$ checks whether the prediction contains a
substantive mathematical primitive rather than a vacuous response, such
as generic advice, a bare technique name, or computation without a
conceptual claim
(Figure [8](#A1.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ A.5 Prompt on Extracting a Mathematical Primitive and Primitive Scoring ‣ Appendix A Data Curation Details ‣ 6 Conclusion ‣ On-Policy Self-Distillation. ‣ 5 Related Work ‣ 4.4 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models")).
For predictions that pass this check, we separately assess the
correctness of the GATE and MECHANISM components using the reference
solution and gold primitive
(Figure [9](#A1.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ A.5 Prompt on Extracting a Mathematical Primitive and Primitive Scoring ‣ Appendix A Data Curation Details ‣ 6 Conclusion ‣ On-Policy Self-Distillation. ‣ 5 Related Work ‣ 4.4 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models")).
The GATE score $`\sigma_{\mathrm{gate}}`$ measures whether the
prediction identifies the essential problem-specific idea, the “what”
that unlocks the problem, while the MECHANISM score
$`\sigma_{\mathrm{mech}}`$ measures whether it correctly explains the
high-level “how,” namely why that idea enables a valid solution
principle. Both correctness judgments emphasize semantic agreement
rather than exact reproduction and do not penalize missing downstream
execution details.

## Appendix B Additional Details on Diagnostic Evaluation

### B.1 Comparison with Full-HLE Performance

Notably, the absolute answer accuracies in
Table [B.3.1](#A2.SS3.SSS1 "B.3.1 Performance across Primitive Families ‣ B.3 Additional Experiment Results ‣ Appendix B Additional Details on Diagnostic Evaluation ‣ 6 Conclusion ‣ On-Policy Self-Distillation. ‣ 5 Related Work ‣ 4.4 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models")
are substantially higher than the commonly reported performance of these
model families on the full HLE benchmark. This difference should not be
interpreted as a contradiction, for two reasons: ❶ Prim is a curated
scorable subset rather than the full HLE distribution; and ❷ during
benchmark construction, human experts removed examples with annotation
noise or evaluation ambiguity in the original HLE ([Center for AI Safety
et al., 2026](#bib.bib1)) and HLE-Verified ([Zhai et al.,
2026](#bib.bib2)) sources, including fundamentally incorrect reference
answers, logical gaps in rationales, and irregular formatting that
hinders automated evaluation.

### B.2 Prompt on Generating the Primitive and Plan using GPT-5.4

We use GPT-5.4 to generate two forms of teacher guidance for the
Execution analysis: a Teacher Primitive, which captures the load-bearing
mathematical structure following
Definition [1](#Thmtheorem1 "Definition 1 (Mathematical Primitive). ‣ 2.1 Mathematical Primitive ‣ 2 Mathematical Primitives as Structural Understanding ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models"),
and a Teacher Plan, which provides a step-by-step solution outline. The
prompts used to generate these two forms of guidance are provided below
in Figures
[10](#A2.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ B.2 Prompt on Generating the Primitive and Plan using GPT-5.4 ‣ Appendix B Additional Details on Diagnostic Evaluation ‣ 6 Conclusion ‣ On-Policy Self-Distillation. ‣ 5 Related Work ‣ 4.4 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models")
and
[11](#A2.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ B.2 Prompt on Generating the Primitive and Plan using GPT-5.4 ‣ Appendix B Additional Details on Diagnostic Evaluation ‣ 6 Conclusion ‣ On-Policy Self-Distillation. ‣ 5 Related Work ‣ 4.4 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models").

conditioning on self-generated primitives provides little or no benefit
and often degrades performance, whereas externally supplied teacher
primitives substantially improve Execution across model families, with
gold primitives yielding the largest gains. These results further
support that the rescue effect is not a consequence of simply
decomposing generation into a discover-then-execute pipeline; rather,
successful execution depends on supplying the relevant mathematical
structure that the model often fails to identify on its own.

#### B.3.4 Failure Decomposition and Rescue Analysis

Table [B.3.3](#A2.SS3.SSS3 "B.3.3 Execution under Different Primitive Sources ‣ B.3.2 Reasoning Length and Generation Behavior ‣ B.3.1 Performance across Primitive Families ‣ B.3 Additional Experiment Results ‣ Appendix B Additional Details on Diagnostic Evaluation ‣ 6 Conclusion ‣ On-Policy Self-Distillation. ‣ 5 Related Work ‣ 4.4 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models")
provides the full model-wise breakdown underlying
Figure [4](#S3.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models").
Across model families, Generation failures are concentrated in the
$`D^{-}`$ regimes. This decomposition further clarifies the role of
primitive discovery: even when overall solving ability is relatively
strong, a substantial portion of failures arises because the model
cannot independently identify the relevant mathematical structure,
despite being able to execute it once supplied.

We further examine how Digestion relates to a model’s ability to make
use of externally supplied primitive guidance.
Table [B.3.4](#A2.SS3.SSS4 "B.3.4 Failure Decomposition and Rescue Analysis ‣ B.3.3 Execution under Different Primitive Sources ‣ B.3.2 Reasoning Length and Generation Behavior ‣ B.3.1 Performance across Primitive Families ‣ B.3 Additional Experiment Results ‣ Appendix B Additional Details on Diagnostic Evaluation ‣ 6 Conclusion ‣ On-Policy Self-Distillation. ‣ 5 Related Work ‣ 4.4 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models")
partitions initially failed problems according to whether the model can
correctly recover the primitive from the reference solution, and then
measures the rescue rate after supplying the teacher primitive. For most
models, digestible failures are substantially more likely to be rescued
than undigestible ones, suggesting that the ability to recover
mathematical structure from a completed solution is closely related to
the ability to incorporate that structure into downstream reasoning.
This relationship is particularly clear for the Qwen3.5 models, where
digestible problems exhibit rescue-rate advantages of 17.6–28.6
percentage points. The pattern is weaker for the DeepSeek-R1 distill
models and is noisy for models with very few undigestible examples,
indicating that Digestion and successful execution are related but
distinct capabilities.

presents the detailed composition of the 709 Mathematics Ph.D.
qualifying examination problems used for our post-training experiments,
categorized by source university and mathematical domain. The problems
span 1991–2026 and are strictly parsed into LaTEX. We select
qualifying-examination problems because their difficulty and open-ended
reasoning demands closely match those of Prim, requiring substantial
mathematical maturity and structural reasoning rather than short-form
answer prediction. Accordingly, the dataset consists entirely of
open-ended proof problems without algorithmically verifiable

extracted from that proof by GPT-5.4-High using the curation prompt of
