## Appendix D Post-Training Setup

All Absorb and OPSD runs use the same training recipe and differ in the
privileged context provided to the teacher: Absorb uses the mathematical
primitive, whereas OPSD uses the reference solution. Training uses the
709 qualifying-examination problems, each paired with a one-sentence
primitive. For each problem, the student generates one on-policy rollout
from the problem alone using temperature $`1.0`$, top-$`p`$ $`0.95`$,
top-$`k`$ $`20`$, a maximum of 4096 completion tokens, and a total
context length of 6144. The teacher uses the same base model with the
adapter disabled and is conditioned on the corresponding privileged
context.

For Absorb, we optimize $`\mathcal{L}_{\textsc{Absorb}{}}`$ with
top-$`K`$ support $`K=128`$ and clamp threshold $`\tau=0.06`$, applied
to all generated completion tokens, including truncated rollouts. We
train LoRA adapters with rank $`64`$ and $`\alpha=128`$ on all attention
and MLP projections, including the linear-attention projections in
Qwen3.5. Optimization uses fused AdamW without weight decay, a learning
rate of $`5\times 10^{-6}`$ with linear scheduling and no warmup,
gradient clipping at $`0.1`$, and an effective batch size of $`32`$ with
per-device batch size $`1`$ and gradient accumulation. Training uses
bf16, gradient checkpointing, and seed $`42`$. Each model is trained for
one epoch, corresponding to $`22`$–$`23`$ optimizer steps. On-policy
rollouts are generated with a co-located vLLM engine synchronized with
the student after every optimizer step.

## Appendix E Post-Training Ablation Studies

To validate the design choices of Absorb, we conduct ablation studies on
the Qwen3.5-9B baseline using Prim ($`n=182`$). We organize the analysis
around three questions: what information should be provided to the
teacher as privilege, how that privileged guidance should be transferred
to the student, and whether the primitive should instead be learned as
an explicit prediction target. For all comparisons, we report Generation
and Discovery together with absolute changes relative to the base model.

|                              |                   |                   |
| ---------------------------- | ----------------- | ----------------- |
| Variant                      | Generation        | Discovery         |
| Qwen3.5-9B (base)            | $`38.46`$         | $`13.19`$         |
| Solution privilege           | $`33.52`$ (-4.95) | $`10.99`$ (-2.20) |
| Primitive privilege (Absorb) | $`43.96`$ (+5.49) | $`14.29`$ (+1.10) |

Table 13: Ablation on the source of privileged information using
Qwen3.5-9B. The training objective is held fixed while the teacher is
conditioned on either the full reference solution or the mathematical
primitive.

##### Teacher Conditioning

Table [13](#A5.T13 "Table 13 ‣ Appendix E Post-Training Ablation Studies ‣ B.3.5 Repairability across Failure Modes ‣ B.3.4 Failure Decomposition and Rescue Analysis ‣ B.3.3 Execution under Different Primitive Sources ‣ B.3.2 Reasoning Length and Generation Behavior ‣ B.3.1 Performance across Primitive Families ‣ B.3 Additional Experiment Results ‣ Appendix B Additional Details on Diagnostic Evaluation ‣ 6 Conclusion ‣ On-Policy Self-Distillation. ‣ 5 Related Work ‣ 4.4 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models")
isolates the effect of the teacher’s privileged input. In both variants,
the student follows the same on-policy solution rollout and is trained
with the same Absorb objective; the only difference is whether the
teacher conditions on the full reference solution or on the mathematical
primitive. Under this controlled comparison, solution conditioning
reduces Generation from $`38.46`$ to $`33.52`$, whereas primitive
conditioning improves it to $`43.96`$. Discovery follows the same trend.
This shows that the gain does not arise from privileged conditioning
alone: the primitive provides a more targeted supervisory signal than
the full solution.

##### Transfer Mechanism

Table [14](#A5.T14 "Table 14 ‣ Transfer Mechanism ‣ Appendix E Post-Training Ablation Studies ‣ B.3.5 Repairability across Failure Modes ‣ B.3.4 Failure Decomposition and Rescue Analysis ‣ B.3.3 Execution under Different Primitive Sources ‣ B.3.2 Reasoning Length and Generation Behavior ‣ B.3.1 Performance across Primitive Families ‣ B.3 Additional Experiment Results ‣ Appendix B Additional Details on Diagnostic Evaluation ‣ 6 Conclusion ‣ On-Policy Self-Distillation. ‣ 5 Related Work ‣ 4.4 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models")
fixes the mathematical primitive as the teacher’s privileged input and
keeps the student rollout in solution space, while varying how the
primitive-conditioned teacher signal is transferred. The _rKL, no cap_
variant applies reverse KL without restricting teacher-induced changes,
providing the unconstrained baseline. The _fKL, capped_ variant instead
uses forward KL on the teacher’s top-$`K`$ support while retaining the
same cap, testing whether the benefit comes simply from limiting large
contributions rather than from the asymmetric reverse-KL formulation.
Both variants underperform the base model, with Generation dropping to
$`31.87`$ and $`36.81`$, respectively.

|                           |                   |                   |
| ------------------------- | ----------------- | ----------------- |
| Transfer Mechanism        | Generation        | Discovery         |
| Qwen3.5-9B (base)         | $`38.46`$         | $`13.19`$         |
| rKL, no cap               | $`31.87`$ (-6.59) | $`10.44`$ (-2.75) |
| fKL, capped               | $`36.81`$ (-1.65) | $`12.09`$ (-1.10) |
| Divergence control        | $`34.62`$ (-3.85) | $`12.09`$ (-1.10) |
| Entropy control           | $`31.87`$ (-6.59) | $`14.29`$ (+1.10) |
| Bounded override (Absorb) | $`43.96`$ (+5.49) | $`14.29`$ (+1.10) |

Table 14: Ablation on mechanisms for transferring primitive-guided
teacher supervision using Qwen3.5-9B. All variants use the mathematical
primitive as privileged information.

_Divergence control_ tests whether harmful transfer can be identified
purely by the magnitude of teacher–student disagreement. Let

|     |                                                                                                                                                    |     |
| --- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle D_{t}=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\bar{\pi}_{S}(\cdot\mid\hat{y}_{<t},x)\;\middle\|\;\bar{\pi}_{T}(\cdot\mid\hat{y}_{<t},x,p)\right),`$ |     |

where both distributions are renormalized. Since the divergence
distribution is highly concentrated in a small tail, we mask tokens
whose divergence exceeds the offline $`95`$th-percentile threshold:

|     |                                                                                                        |     |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle m_{t}^{\mathrm{div}}=\mathbf{1}\!\left[D_{t}\leq\tau_{D}\right],\qquad\tau_{D}=0.05.`$ |     |

This removes only about $`5\%`$ of tokens but approximately $`86\%`$ of
the total divergence mass, partially recovering Generation from
$`31.87`$ to $`34.62`$.

_Entropy control_ tests a finer hypothesis: whether harmful overrides
and useful primitive guidance can be separated within this
high-divergence tail using the student’s confidence. We define the
student’s full-vocabulary entropy as

|     |                                                                                                |     |
| --- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle H_{t}=-\sum_{v}\pi_{S}(v\mid\hat{y}_{<t},x)\log\pi_{S}(v\mid\hat{y}_{<t},x),`$ |     |

and mask only high-divergence, low-entropy positions:

|     |                                                                                                                                 |     |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle m_{t}^{\mathrm{ent}}=\mathbf{1}\!\left[D_{t}\leq\tau_{D}\;\lor\;H_{t}\geq\tau_{H}\right],\qquad\tau_{H}=0.86.`$ |     |

This preserves high-divergence positions where the student is uncertain,
under the hypothesis that these are more likely to contain useful
primitive-specific guidance. However, despite masking fewer tokens,
Generation returns to $`31.87`$, indicating that neither divergence
magnitude nor student confidence cleanly separates beneficial from
harmful teacher intervention.

In contrast, Absorb avoids making a whole-token keep-or-drop decision.
Its bounded override operates within each token distribution, retaining
supervision at every position while limiting how strongly individual
teacher preferences can suppress student-supported choices. This is the
only transfer mechanism in the comparison that improves over the base
model, reaching $`43.96`$ Generation.

##### Rollout Target

Table [15](#A5.T15 "Table 15 ‣ Rollout Target ‣ Appendix E Post-Training Ablation Studies ‣ B.3.5 Repairability across Failure Modes ‣ B.3.4 Failure Decomposition and Rescue Analysis ‣ B.3.3 Execution under Different Primitive Sources ‣ B.3.2 Reasoning Length and Generation Behavior ‣ B.3.1 Performance across Primitive Families ‣ B.3 Additional Experiment Results ‣ Appendix B Additional Details on Diagnostic Evaluation ‣ 6 Conclusion ‣ On-Policy Self-Distillation. ‣ 5 Related Work ‣ 4.4 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models")
isolates whether the mathematical primitive should serve as privileged
guidance or as the student’s rollout target. In the Absorb setting, the
student continues to generate solutions while the primitive is available
only to the teacher. We compare this against variants in which the
student instead generates the primitive itself under uncapped reverse
KL, capped forward KL, or the same capped reverse-KL objective used by
Absorb. Primitive-target rollouts remain weak across all three
objectives. Even under the Absorb objective, changing only the rollout
target from solution to primitive yields $`39.01`$ Generation, compared
with $`43.96`$ when the primitive instead conditions the teacher while
the student generates solutions. This indicates that the primitive is
more effective as privileged guidance that shapes solution reasoning
than as the object the student is directly optimized to produce.

|                            |                   |                   |
| -------------------------- | ----------------- | ----------------- |
| Rollout Target / Objective | Generation        | Discovery         |
| Qwen3.5-9B (base)          | $`38.46`$         | $`13.19`$         |
| Absorb                     | $`43.96`$ (+5.49) | $`14.29`$ (+1.10) |
| rKL, no cap                | $`32.97`$ (-5.49) | $`13.19`$ (+0.00) |
| fKL, capped                | $`33.52`$ (-4.95) | $`9.34`$ (-3.85)  |
| rKL, capped                | $`39.01`$ (+0.55) | $`12.09`$ (-1.10) |

Absorb baseline keeps the student in solution-generation space and uses
the primitive only as privileged teacher information; the remaining

under different distillation objectives.

##### Alternative Training Objectives

Table [16](#A5.T16 "Table 16 ‣ Alternative Training Objectives ‣ Appendix E Post-Training Ablation Studies ‣ B.3.5 Repairability across Failure Modes ‣ B.3.4 Failure Decomposition and Rescue Analysis ‣ B.3.3 Execution under Different Primitive Sources ‣ B.3.2 Reasoning Length and Generation Behavior ‣ B.3.1 Performance across Primitive Families ‣ B.3 Additional Experiment Results ‣ Appendix B Additional Details on Diagnostic Evaluation ‣ 6 Conclusion ‣ On-Policy Self-Distillation. ‣ 5 Related Work ‣ 4.4 Experimental Results ‣ 4 Internalizing Primitive-Guided Reasoning ‣ 3.3 Further Analysis: Which Failures Are Repairable? ‣ 3.2 Results Analysis ‣ 3.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 3 Diagnosing Mathematical Reasoning ‣ The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models")
compares Absorb against alternative post-training objectives on the same
Qwen3.5-9B backbone. We separate the comparison into teacher-guided
distillation objectives and direct supervised fine-tuning objectives.

Among the distillation baselines, *TOP-D* ([Xie et al.,
2026](#bib.bib30)) is a policy-gradient on-policy distillation method
based on a bounded proximal reward. We adapt it to our setting using the
same 709-problem training corpus, primitive privilege, and self-teacher
as Absorb, with $`G=4`$ student rollouts per prompt, proximal reward

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\tilde{r}_{t}=\log\!\left(\alpha\rho_{t}+1-\alpha\right),\qquad\alpha=0.1,
``` |  |

followed by token-level length-normalized future returns and
group-normalized advantages. Despite operating with the same privileged
signal, TOP-D reduces Generation to $`31.87`$ and Discovery to $`9.34`$,
indicating that the primitive alone is insufficient without an
appropriate transfer mechanism.

*Dual-channel* is an alternative design motivated by our analysis of
rescued trajectories, which suggested that primitive guidance primarily
acts through early route selection and later adjudication. The route
channel applies reverse KL only to the first 512 completion tokens. The
adjudication channel operates at student-generated self-doubt forks
(e.g., “Wait”, “But”, “However”, “Actually”) and asks the student to
sample candidate continuations. The primitive-conditioned teacher
provides only a preference over these student-generated candidates
rather than generating tokens itself. Given teacher and frozen-base
scores $`z_{T}`$ and $`z_{0}`$, we form the base-corrected teacher
preference

|     |                                                                   |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       q_{T}=\operatorname{softmax}\left(\frac{z_{T}-z_{0}}{0.2}\right),
       ```                                                                |     |

and optimize

|     |                                                                   |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{adj}}=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_{T}\parallel q_{S}),
       ```                                                                |     |

with weight $`0.3`$ in addition to the early-route reverse-KL term.
Because this variant uses a larger 1,692-problem pool, full-length
primitive annotations, and 8k-token completions, it should be
interpreted as a reference alternative rather than a strict
single-variable ablation. It nevertheless substantially underperforms
both the base model and Absorb.

We separately compare direct supervised objectives. *Solution SFT*
fine-tunes the model on the human-authored reference solutions, while
*primitive SFT* directly trains the model to generate the mathematical
primitive. Solution SFT lowers Generation to $`32.42`$, and primitive
SFT performs worst overall, reducing Generation and Discovery to
$`28.02`$ and $`2.75`$, respectively. Together, these results show that
neither alternative teacher-guided distillation nor direct supervision
on solutions or primitives substitutes for the combination used by
Absorb: primitive-conditioned teacher guidance transferred through
bounded override while the student remains in solution-generation space.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
| Training Objective | Generation | Discovery |
| Qwen3.5-9B (base) | $`38.46`$ | $`13.19`$ |
| Absorb | $`43.96`$ (+5.49) | $`14.29`$ (+1.10) |
| Teacher-guided distillation |  |  |
| TOP-D ([Xie et al., 2026](#bib.bib30)) | $`31.87`$ (-6.59) | $`9.34`$ (-3.85) |
| Dual-channel^(†) | $`29.67`$ (-8.79) | $`10.44`$ (-2.75) |
| Direct supervised fine-tuning |  |  |
| Solution SFT | $`32.42`$ (-6.04) | $`12.64`$ (-0.55) |
| Primitive SFT | $`28.02`$ (-10.44) | $`2.75`$ (-10.44) |
````
